proposed.author: EditorDavid
proposed.description: The Register writes that "The worst of the patchpocalypse may be behind us, according to Linus Torvalds." In his weekly kernel update post, Torvalds said Linux 7.4 rc2 was a big release partly because it contained code he'd left out of rc1 because he'd been busy and it was already the largest such release in kernel history. But Torvalds said the other reason rc2 was big was "various AI fixes." Such fixes are necessary because ever since Anthropic launched its Mythos bug-finding model in April, developers have been able to find more software flaws than was previously possible. Microsoft, for example, addressed a record 974 flaws in September — its third record fixing spree this year after it whacked 622 flaws in July and 206 in June. Oracle addressed 1,449 flaws in a single month. That's many more patches than IT teams are set up to handle, yet they must find ways to deal with bugs more quickly because attackers are increasingly targeting flaws found by AI. Torvalds' post suggests that, perhaps, the worst of this is behind us. "This time around Alexei claims that on the bpf side at least the fixes are now coming in faster than the new reports, and that sounds lovely if true," he wrote. That's a reference to Alexei Starovoitov, co-creator and lead dev on the Extended Berkeley Packet Filter (eBPF), the project that makes it possible to run sandboxed programs within the Linux kerne
proposed.title: Linus Torvalds Wonders If Linux's AI-Prompted Patch Flood Has Peaked

proposed.description: Getting a transcript is only the first handoff in a caption editor. After that, the words have to survive several clocks, a live preview, a style system, and a video encoder. I’m building Karaoke Captions , a React and TypeScript editor that transcribes and renders video locally. In an earlier post I gave an overview of the product. This time I want to walk through the implementation choices that make a word-by-word caption become a finished MP4. The interesting parts are the boundaries: compressed media to PCM, model output to editable timing, preview time to export time, and decoded frames to an MP4 container. The pipeline I keep separate from the interface The local workflow has six main stages: File / Blob → decode audio to 16 kHz mono Float32 PCM → transcribe in a Web Worker → normalise word timestamps and build phrases → edit text, timing and style → draw captions over decoded video frames → encode and mux the finished MP4 React owns the editing interface. The document holds the words and style choices. The transcription worker handles model work. The rendering code decides what a caption looks like at a given time. That separation lets me revise a font or a sentence without running speech recognition again. It also gives the preview and export a shared description of the video they’re supposed to produce. 1. proposed.author: Віталік Бакута
proposed.description: Quick question: when you last converted a HEIC to JPG or merged two PDFs, where did that file go? For most "free online converters" the answer is: their server . Your passport scan, your contract, your private photos, uploaded to who-knows-where. Here's the thing: in 2026 this is completely unnecessary. Browsers can do almost all of it locally. What modern browsers can do without a server Image conversion : Canvas API + WebAssembly decoders (HEIC, AVIF, even RAW formats) PDF manipulation : merge, split, rotate, compress, all in JS 3D file viewing : STL, STEP, OBJ, GLB via WebGL Dev utilities : JSON ⇄ YAML, Base64, regex, UUIDs The file never leaves your device. You can literally turn off Wi-Fi after the page loads and it still works. I built a collection of these FormatMath is 50+ converters and tools, all client-side: HEIC to JPG (the iPhone photo problem, solved) Merge PDF / Compress PDF STEP viewer (surprisingly hard to find a free one) Remove photo metadata : strips GPS location before you post a photo Developer tools : JSON/YAML/CSV, Base64, regex tester No sign-up, no upload, no file size limits. The tradeoff (being honest) Client-side processing depends on the user's device. A 200 MB PDF on an old phone will be slower than on a server. For 95% of everyday tasks, though, it's instant. What's a tool you wish existed in the browser? I'm taking requests. 👇 Also mine: BotRead
proposed.title: Stop uploading your files to random converter sites

proposed.description: An anonymous reader quotes a report from Ars Technica: Nightmare Eclipse, the pseudonym of a researcher with an ongoing, very public beef with Microsoft, has dropped yet another Windows zero-day. On Tuesday, Nightmare Eclipse disclosed SignDrop, a vulnerability that gives local users full System rights on some versions of Windows. The vulnerability resides in the Common Log File System, which Microsoft describes as a "general-purpose logging service used by software clients running in user-mode or kernel-mode." By forcing a privileged process such as Windows Defender to open a crafted CLFS container, an attacker with ordinary user rights can abuse the privileged file creation to elevate privileges to System. [...] Researcher Will Dormann said in an interview that he has been able to reproduce the exploit and that it works as described, but not on all versions of Windows 11. But there's a catch, he said. "The requirements are important in that it seems to require Windows 26H2, and one that has existed for more than 90 days, it seems," he explained. "That is, you can't just take a new 26H2 system and install updates and have it work." For a system to be vulnerable, Dormann said, the HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\CLFS\Authentication\Mode value must be 0 or 1." Of the many machines Dormann uses, only a single one met this requirement. Microsoft said in a stat
proposed.title: Windows 0-Day Dropped By Disgruntled Researcher Hands Hackers System Rights

proposed.description: Last month I noticed something weird: my site ranked fine on Google, but when I asked ChatGPT, Claude and Perplexity about my topic, they never mentioned it. Not once. So I dug in. Turns out there's a whole layer of "AI visibility" most of us never check. What I found 1. My robots.txt was blocking AI crawlers I didn't even know existed. There are 20+ AI bots now: GPTBot, ClaudeBot, PerplexityBot, Google-Extended, and more. Some hosting setups and security plugins block them by default. Cloudflare can too. 2. My content was rendered with JavaScript. Many AI crawlers don't execute JS the way Googlebot does. If your content only appears after hydration, some bots see an empty page. 3. No structured data. Schema markup helps AI systems understand what your page is: a product, an article, a tool. How to check your own site (2 minutes) I ended up building a set of free checkers for this: BotReady . A few worth trying: AI Crawler Checker : tests your robots.txt against 21 AI bots AI Crawlability Checker : shows what a bot actually sees on your page AI SEO Analysis : 40 checks and a score 5 free checks a day, no sign-up. Quick fixes if you're blocked User-agent: GPTBot Allow: / User-agent: ClaudeBot Allow: / User-agent: PerplexityBot Allow: / (Only if you want AI tools to use your content. That's a real choice, not a default.) Your turn Run your site through a checker and drop your res
proposed.title: Your website might be invisible to ChatGPT (and you'd never know)
